In the minimally controlled models, the estimated relationship between Chinese import exposure and Republican presidential margins becomes more positive in 2016 and 2020 relative to 1988. The estimates approach zero with core controls and become slightly negative with full controls. We therefore find no robust positive association across specifications.

The differences across specifications suggest that initial industrial and demographic characteristics are important when interpreting the relationship. Because our political analysis uses observed exposure rather than the instrumental-variables approach of ADH's labor-market study, we cannot interpret these associations as causal effects. Aggregate election results also cannot establish whether residents changed their preferences, whether electoral participation shifted, or whether migration changed the composition of the electorate.

Future research using individual voting data, migration records, and measures of political mobilization could help distinguish these explanations.
